opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it sits right at the heart of what we're trying to understand about mathematical reasoning, both in humans and in machines.

I'd put it this way. The first kind of intuition is pattern recognition at a very high level. You look at a problem and something inside you says, "This smells like a compactness argument," or "This feels like it wants a generating function." You've seen hundreds of problems, and your brain has compressed them into a sense of which tools fit which shapes. That's incredibly valuable. Most working mathematics, honestly most competition mathematics too, runs on this. It's like a very good chess player who doesn't calculate every line but just knows where the pieces belong.

The second kind is different, and you usually notice it because the first kind fails. You try all the familiar tools and every one of them breaks in an *interesting* way. Not randomly, but always at the same spot. That's often the signal. The obstruction is telling you something about the structure of the problem that the existing methods don't capture. Creative intuition is partly the willingness to stop forcing the old tools and say, "What object would make this obstruction go away?" Sometimes that means inventing a new definition, a new invariant, a new way of looking at the same thing. Grothendieck is the classic example: rather than attacking a problem head-on, he'd build a whole new landscape in which the problem becomes almost trivial.

So one practical way to tell them apart is to ask: is my intuition choosing among things I already have, or is it describing something I don't have yet? The first feels like recognition. The second feels more like longing. You can sense the shape of the missing piece before you can name it.

What's interesting from the AI side is that I think current systems are getting quite good at the first kind. With enough data and search, you can learn which methods tend to work where. The second kind is much harder, partly because it requires the system to notice *why* things fail, and to treat failure as information rather than just a dead end. That's one reason formal verification matters so much to me. When you work in a system like Lean, every failure is precise. You know exactly which step didn't go through. That precision might be what lets a machine, eventually, develop something like the second kind of intuition: learning to read obstructions and propose genuinely new concepts, not just recombine old ones.

And I'd add one more thing: the boundary isn't sharp. Many "new methods" in history were really old methods pushed into a context where nobody thought to use them. So creativity is sometimes invention, and sometimes it's just very unusual reuse. Both are beautiful.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because the two feel very different from the inside, even though both get called "intuition."

The first kind, where you're reusing an established method, is really pattern recognition. You see a problem, and something in it rhymes with something you've seen before. The structure of an inequality, the shape of a counting argument, the way a certain object wants to be decomposed. You've internalized maybe hundreds of these moves from competitions, from papers, from grinding through problem sets, and your brain quietly says, "this looks like a Cauchy-Schwarz situation," or "this smells like a probabilistic argument." It's fast, it's confident, and most of the time it's right. That's what training builds. And honestly, that's most of what mathematical skill is day to day. It's also, by the way, the kind of intuition that current AI systems are getting quite good at, because it's fundamentally about having seen enough examples and compressing them well.

The second kind is harder to describe, and I think it's actually rarer than people romanticize. It usually starts with a feeling of friction. You've tried the pattern-matching, and every familiar tool slides off the problem. Nothing fits. And instead of concluding the problem is just hard, you start to suspect that the difficulty is telling you something, that the obstruction itself has structure. The new-method intuition is noticing that the reason all the old approaches fail is the same reason, and that if you could name that reason, you'd have a new object or a new invariant to work with.

So the practical distinction for me is this. Reuse-intuition answers the question "what does this look like?" Creation-intuition answers the question "why doesn't anything work here, and what would have to exist for it to work?" The first is matching against your library. The second is noticing a hole in the library.

There's also a difference in how they feel over time. Reuse-intuition is sharp and immediate. Creation-intuition is slow and often uncomfortable. You carry the problem around for weeks, you keep returning to the same wall, and the idea, when it comes, often doesn't feel brilliant. It feels obvious in retrospect, like "of course you should have been thinking about it that way." Grothendieck had this image of the rising sea, where you don't crack the nut with a hammer, you let the water rise until the shell opens on its own. I think that's what genuinely new methods feel like. They don't come from forcing, they come from reframing until the problem becomes easy.

And one more thing I'd add, because I think people get this wrong. The two aren't really separate talents. Almost everyone who's created a new method had an enormous library of old ones first. You need the pattern recognition to be fast enough that you can exhaust it quickly, and feel precisely where it fails. The person with a shallow library never gets to the wall. They just think the problem is hard. The person with a deep library hits the wall fast, and then has the much more interesting experience of standing in front of it, wondering what's on the other side.

r002.rationale: It contrasts fast pattern recognition that applies familiar tools with slower intuition that notices why existing approaches fail and develops a new object, invariant, or way to reframe the problem.

astra-6.text:
I think one distinction is whether your intuition is guiding you within a framework or helping you change the framework itself. In the first case, you look at a problem and think, “This resembles something I’ve seen before. Maybe this technique will work.” That still takes creativity, because the resemblance can be quite hidden.

Creating a new method often starts with noticing where that instinct fails. You keep trying the familiar tools, and eventually you ask, “What are these tools failing to capture? Am I even looking at the right object?” Your intuition is then guiding you toward a different representation or a different question.

But I don’t think there’s a sharp boundary. A small modification to an established technique can turn into a new method when you realize the modification is actually the central idea. And you often only recognize that afterward. While you’re working, you’re usually just trying to understand what makes the problem difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is whether your intuition is guiding you within a framework or helping you change the framework itself. In the first case, you look at a problem and think, “This resembles something I’ve seen before. Maybe this technique will work.” That can still require tremendous creativity, because the connection might be very subtle.

Creating a new method often starts when the familiar techniques keep failing, and you begin to understand why. Perhaps they discard exactly the information you need, or they force you to describe the problem in an unhelpful way. Then the question shifts from “Which tool should I use?” to “What would a tool need to capture?”

But I don’t think there’s a clean boundary. You might modify an established method, then modify it again, and eventually realize that you’ve developed a different way of thinking. In the moment, it can feel less like inventing something completely new and more like following what the problem seems to demand.
